Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes the dot products of the query with all keys, divides each by √d_k, and applies a softmax function to obtain weights on the values [P1]. The input consists of queries and keys of dimension d_k, and values of dimension d_v [P1]. The authors divide by √d_k to counteract the effect of dot products growing large in magnitude for large values of d_k [P2]. This growth pushes the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients [P2]. The scaling factor distinguishes their algorithm from standard dot-product attention [P1]. The final output is computed as the weighted sum of the values using these attention weights [P3].

The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three different ways: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention, and decoder self-attention [P1]. In encoder-decoder attention layers, queries come from the previous decoder layer while memory keys and values come from the encoder output, allowing every decoder position to attend to all input positions [P1]. The encoder contains self-attention layers where keys, values, and queries all originate from the output of the previous encoder layer, enabling each position to attend to all positions in that previous layer [P1]. Similarly, decoder self-attention layers allow each position to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position [P1]. This specific arrangement in the decoder is necessary to prevent leftward information flow and preserve the auto-regressive property [P1]. Multi-head attention generally allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions [P4].

The Transformer requires positional encoding because the model contains no recurrence and no convolution, necessitating the injection of information about the relative or absolute position of tokens [P1]. The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they hypothesized this function would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions [P1]. Additionally, the sinusoidal version was selected because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training [P2]. The authors noted that learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results to the sinusoidal version [P2]. This finding is supported by experiments where replacing sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings yielded nearly identical results to the base model [P3].

Moshi aims to solve the limitations of latency, the textual information bottleneck, and turn-based modeling [P2]. Conventional turn-based paradigms fall short in modeling interruptions, overlapping speech, and backchanneling [P2]. The model addresses the need to run in real time and allow for long conversations in full-duplex [P3]. It is designed to be speech-to-speech to handle paralinguistic communication [P3]. Moshi also aims to display knowledge and reasoning abilities for helpful and enjoyable conversations [P3].

Current systems for spoken dialogue rely on pipelines of independent components, which induces a latency of several seconds between interactions [P2]. Because text serves as the intermediate modality in these frameworks, non-linguistic information such as emotion or non-speech sounds is lost during the interaction [P2]. These systems also rely on a segmentation into speaker turns, which fails to account for overlapping speech, interruptions, and interjections [P2].

Conventional spoken dialogue systems suffer from high latency, often reaching several seconds, which contrasts with the few hundred milliseconds typical of natural conversations [P2]. These systems rely on text as an intermediate modality, causing them to ignore non-linguistic information such as emotion, accent, and non-speech audio [P2]. Finally, they are fundamentally turn-based, which prevents them from effectively modeling conversational dynamics like interruptions, overlapping speech, and backchanneling [P2].

Helium is a bespoke text language model backbone built from scratch to provide strong reasoning abilities to the system [P1][P4]. Mimi is a neural audio codec that uses residual vector quantization and distills semantic knowledge from a self-supervised speech model [P1]. Mimi operates as a fully causal tokenizer at a low framerate and bitrate, which is crucial for achieving the low latency required for real-time dialogue [P2]. Moshi is the overarching multi-stream speech-to-speech Transformer model that enables full-duplex spoken dialogue [P4]. The architecture allows Moshi to speak and listen to the user simultaneously without explicitly modeling speaker turns [P4]. Moshi utilizes Inner Monologue to jointly model text and audio tokens, allowing it to exploit the knowledge imparted by the text modality while remaining a speech-to-speech system [P4]. [P1]

The architecture combines Helium with a smaller Transformer to predict audio tokens in a hierarchical and streaming fashion [P4]. Moshi jointly models the audio streams from both the user and the system, along with Moshi’s text tokens, using a Depth Transformer [P3]. This multi-stream design allows the model to speak and listen simultaneously without explicitly modeling speaker turns [P3].

The architecture uses Mimi to capture user input audio and Moshi's output voice with high quality and efficiency [P4]. Moshi jointly models the audio streams from both the user and Moshi, along with Moshi's text tokens, using a Depth Transformer compatible with streaming inference [P4]. This integration allows Moshi to exploit the knowledge imparted from the text modality via Inner Monologue while remaining a speech-to-speech system [P4].

Inner Monologue is a training and inference setup that predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens to improve factuality and linguistic quality [P1]. It decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic, and acoustic tokens, predicting this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner [P3]. This approach uses text tokens as a per-timestep prefix to the semantic token, extending the coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy [P2]. The method significantly improves the length and quality of generated speech by leveraging this structured prediction [P2]. Additionally, Inner Monologue allows representing all utterances as both text and speech without switching modalities [P3]. This hierarchical modeling decomposes the generation task without increasing the sequence length of the Transformer outputs [P3].

Inner Monologue is a training and inference setup for audio language models that predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens [P1]. This mechanism significantly improves the factuality and linguistic quality of the generated speech [P1]. The approach extends the coarse-to-fine generation hierarchy by using text tokens as a per-timestep prefix to the semantic token [P1]. Experiments demonstrate that this method drastically improves both the length and quality of the generated speech [P1]. Additionally, Inner Monologue decomposes speech on a per-frame basis, allowing each prediction step to output a speech frame [P2]. This per-frame decomposition makes the model compatible with real-time generation, unlike systems that require generating a complete text sequence first [P2].

Inner Monologue is a training and inference setup that predicts time-aligned text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens to improve the factuality and linguistic quality of generated speech [P3]. It decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic, and acoustic tokens, predicting this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner [P2]. The text stream is derived from the transcription of Moshi's own audio using the SentencePiece tokenizer and Whisper [P4]. To align with the constant framerate of 12.5Hz, word-level timestamps from Whisper are used to map text tokens to specific time indices [P4]. This mechanism provides a scaffolding that increases the linguistic quality of generation, with ablation studies showing it has one of the most critical impacts on speech quality [P4]. The most drastic improvement to the quality and length of generated speech comes from enabling Inner Monologue [P5].

Moshi achieves full-duplex communication by using a multi-stream architecture that allows the model to speak and listen to the user simultaneously without explicitly modeling speaker turns [P3]. This design enables the handling of full-duplex dialogues with arbitrary dynamics by modeling several audio streams in parallel [P4]. Modeling the user's and system's audio as separate parallel streams is important because previous approaches that model both into a single token stream are challenging in the presence of significant overlap [P1]. The multi-stream approach allows for a conceptually and practically simple handling of these complex dialogue dynamics [P4]. Unlike previous full-duplex systems that may not run online or lack text knowledge, Moshi's architecture supports real-time generation with strong reasoning abilities [P1][P3].

Fixed-vocabulary tokenization is described as a pervasive handcrafted preprocessing step that comes with well-documented drawbacks, including poor character-level understanding and a lack of meaning and interpretability [P3]. The authors note that this process leads to degraded performance on complex languages and modalities [P3]. Additionally, tokenization bias prevents the model from determining if a character is the start of a new word until subsequent characters are observed [P1]. This issue can be exacerbated, as determining whether a specific character is the start of a token may require knowing the next two bytes [P1]. Replacing the tokenization–LM–detokenization pipeline with a single end-to-end model would better adhere to the spirit of deep learning and potentially scale more powerfully [P3].

The authors identify that fixed-vocabulary tokenization is a pervasive handcrafted preprocessing step that comes with well-documented drawbacks [P2]. These drawbacks include poor character-level understanding, a lack of meaning and interpretability, and degraded performance on complex languages and modalities [P2]. Replacing the tokenization–LM–detokenization pipeline with a single end-to-end model would better adhere to the spirit of deep learning [P2]. Such an approach would ideally scale more powerfully with data and parameters, aligning with the concept of the bitter lesson [P2]. However, tokenization remains indispensable for its ability to compress and shorten sequences, as no end-to-end tokenizer-free model has yet matched the performance of tokenizer-based models when matched for computational budget [P2].

Pre-processing steps such as tokenization remain a barrier to true end-to-end foundation models, which motivated the introduction of H-Net [P4]. The authors argue that tokenization implicitly contains next-byte information, a phenomenon termed "tokenization bias" that prevents models from determining word boundaries without seeing subsequent characters [P3]. Fixed-vocabulary tokenizers can leak information about the data mix they were trained on, as shown by examining the vocabulary of a BPE tokenizer [P1]. Additionally, tokenization qualitatively changes what Transformers can learn for certain data distributions, and the primary role of shrinking input sequence length is not the sole factor in model performance [P1]. Schmidt et al. (2024) provided evidence against the hypothesis that tokenization's primary role is to shrink input sequence length by showing that higher compression rates can lead to worse language models [P1]. H-Net addresses these issues by replacing the tokenization–LM–detokenization pipeline with a single model learned fully end-to-end [P4].

H-Net employs a hierarchical architecture comprising three primary components: encoder networks (E), a main network (M), and decoder networks (D) [P1]. In the information flow, raw data is first processed by a small encoder network [P3]. The data is then downsampled and passed through the main network, which operates on compressed chunks [P3]. Finally, the data is upsampled before being passed through a decoder network that operates on the original resolution [P3]. The encoder must simultaneously preserve fine-grained information for transmission to its corresponding decoder via residual connections and compress inputs into chunks for the main network [P2]. The decoder effectively combines coarse-grained representations from the main network with fine-grained details from the encoder residuals [P2].

H-Net employs a hierarchical architecture comprising three primary components: encoder networks (E), a main network (M), and decoder networks (D) [P1]. In a single-stage model, the architecture consists of one encoder network, one main network, and one decoder network [P1]. The encoder networks must simultaneously preserve fine-grained information for transmission to their corresponding decoders via residual connections and compress inputs into chunks of richer representations for the main network [P2]. The main network operates on these progressively compressed sequences, allowing for larger networks within the same computational budget [P3]. The decoder networks effectively combine the coarse-grained representations from the main network with the fine-grained details from the encoder residuals [P2]. Both the encoder and decoder networks operate on uncompressed sequences, which makes computational efficiency a significant design constraint [P2].

H-Net employs a hierarchical architecture comprising three primary components: encoder networks (E), a main network (M), and decoder networks (D) [P1]. The overall pipeline begins with the encoder processing the input sequence, followed by the main network processing the compressed representations, and finally the decoder decompressing the sequence back to its original resolution [P1]. Information flows from the encoder to the main network via a chunking layer that compresses input sequences into fewer vectors with richer semantic embeddings [P1]. The main network operates on these progressively compressed sequences, where the sequence length $L^S$ is much smaller than the initial input length $L^0$ [P2]. The decoder combines coarse-grained representations from the main network with fine-grained details from the encoder residuals to reconstruct the output [P2]. This process is formalized by the equations where the encoder output is chunked, the main network processes the result, and the decoder applies a dechunking operation along with a linear projection of the encoder output [P1].

It prevents the model from overfitting to suboptimal chunking patterns early in training by smoothly interpolating between discrete choices based on confidence scores [P3]. When the smoothing module is removed, compression ratios fluctuate severely throughout training, which prevents the model from learning consistent chunking boundaries [P2]. This instability directly manifests as substantial performance degradation, confirming that smooth gradient flow through the decompression process is crucial for effective end-to-end learning [P2].
